1177.title: Spells of protection (Kern ch. 21)
1177.hook: protective chants for those who keep the sutra
1177.howItsDone: Dharanis are recited in Mahayana and Vajrayana settings, often kept in their Sanskrit-derived sounds rather than translated; in Nichiren Buddhism people chant the sutra's title, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great tongue: the Buddhas confirming the teaching for every world to hear. Your line: confirmed.

Some words are said less for what they mean than for what they do. A lullaby hummed over a crib. A name called across a dark yard. The words a grandmother says when someone sneezes. Chapter twenty-one of the Lotus Sutra, in Kern's numbering, is full of words like that: strings of syllables offered to the Buddha by bodhisattvas, by heavenly kings, and by a band of fierce female spirits, all to guard the people who keep this teaching. A new week opens with them. Today's word: dharani.
screen: `WORDS SAID FOR WHAT THEY DO.` → `STRINGS OF SYLLABLES.` → `TO GUARD THE KEEPERS.`

segments.voice: First, the givers. One after another they rise in the assembly: the bodhisattva Medicine King, whose own story comes tomorrow, another bodhisattva, then two of the great heavenly kings who guard the quarters of the world. Each says, in effect: here is a spell, so that no harm comes to those who preach this teaching. And each recites it. Second, the spells themselves. They are not sentences but runs of sound, kept as sound rather than turned into meanings. The word, dharani, is explained in the tradition as something that holds: holding the teaching in memory, holding the speaker safe. The chant works by being kept and said, the way a lullaby works on a child who understands none of the words. Third, the fierce ones. Then come the rakshasis, female spirits known in Indian stories for doing harm, with Hariti, whom the tradition remembers as a devourer of children turned toward protecting them. Now they stand before the Buddha, promise to guard the keepers of the sutra, and offer a spell of their own. The very beings people feared become the guards at the door. Fourth, the Buddha's answer. He approves each offering. What these spells protect is not treasure or territory but people: whoever keeps the teaching, reads it, and passes it on. Protection, in this chapter, is the circle of care that gathers around someone doing that.
screen: `THE GIVERS RISE ONE BY ONE.` · `SOUNDS MORE THAN SENTENCES.` · `EVEN THE FIERCE ONES GUARD.` · `WHAT THE SPELLS PROTECT.` · then, large: `PROTECTED.`

segments.voice: If you already chant, use a protective line from your own tradition; Nichiren Buddhists, for example, chant this sutra's title, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. If you don't, choose a line from this path you already carry, like I do not despise you, and say it softly on each out-breath. Don't reach for meaning; just keep the line, the way a dharani is kept.
Dharani. A chant of syllables kept and recited for protection and for holding the teaching, offered in the Lotus Sutra to guard its keepers. Today's word.
Your line: protected. Even the fierce ones, once feared, became the guards at the door. Until tomorrow.

1178.title: The Medicine King (Kern ch. 22)
1178.hook: a story of total devotion from a past life; the tradition reads it as an image of offering, never an instruction
1178.howItsDone: In East Asian Buddhism, the Medicine King chapter is recited and studied as a teaching on devotion and on the sutra as medicine; offerings of light, such as lamps and candles set before Buddha images, are part of Buddhist devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dharani: chants of syllables offered to guard the people who keep the teaching, even by the fierce spirits. Your line: protected.

This is a hard story, and it's told here the way this path reads it: as an image, not an instruction. Chapter twenty-two in Kern's numbering goes back to a past life of the bodhisattva called the Medicine King, the one who offered the first spell yesterday. Then he had another name, Sarvasattvapriyadarshana, roughly, the one all beings are glad to see. He had heard this teaching from his Buddha, and he wanted to give an offering that held nothing back.
screen: `A HARD STORY.` → `AN IMAGE, NOT AN INSTRUCTION.` → `AN OFFERING THAT HOLDS NOTHING BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the story. This bodhisattva first offers flowers and incense to his Buddha, then decides that no outward gift is enough. He offers his own body as a lamp, and the light, the sutra says, shines across countless worlds, and the Buddhas there praise the offering. In a later life he offers his arms at the stupas, and by a vow of truth they are restored. It is told in the sutra's large, dreamlike way, with worlds and ages beyond counting. Second, how it is heard here. Buddhist teachers who comment on this chapter have read it in different ways. On this path it is heard as a picture of devotion pushed to its edge, and never as something to do. Nobody here is asked to harm their body. Buddhist precepts begin with not taking life. If this story stirs something heavy for you, please reach out today to someone you trust, or to a local crisis line. In the US, call or text 988, any hour. Third, the medicine. The chapter then praises the sutra itself, and the images are gentle: like fire for someone who is cold, clothing for someone who has none, a boat for someone crossing water, a lamp in the dark, a doctor for the sick. That last one fits the name. The Medicine King is a healer, and the teaching he loves is medicine. Fourth, what remains for an ordinary day. Strip away the vast scale, and the chapter asks a simple question. What would it mean to give something your whole self, not just the leftovers? Most days the answer is small: your full attention, given without holding part of it back.
screen: `AN OFFERING WITH NOTHING HELD BACK.` · `HEARD AS AN IMAGE, NEVER A TASK.` · `A LAMP, A BOAT, A DOCTOR.` · `ATTENTION AS THE OFFERING.` · then, large: `AN OFFERING OF DEVOTION.`

segments.voice: For these two minutes, give your whole attention to one thing, the breath coming in and going out: not half of it while the other half plans dinner, all of it, as an offering. When attention wanders, and it will, bring it back the way you'd set a gift down carefully, not the way you'd correct a mistake. Each return is the offering made again.
The Medicine King. Bhaishajyaraja, the healer bodhisattva of the Lotus Sutra, whose past life is told as an image of devotion with nothing held back. Today's word.
Your line: an offering of devotion. Given whole, not as leftovers. Rest well.

1179.title: Gadgadasvara (Kern ch. 23)
1179.hook: a bodhisattva who appears in many forms to help
1179.howItsDone: In East Asian Buddhism this bodhisattva is known by the Chinese name Wonderful Sound, and the chapter is studied as a teaching on skillful means, the many forms a bodhisattva takes to help.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Medicine King, a story heard as an image of devotion with nothing held back. Your line: an offering of devotion.

Before the visitor arrives, flowers arrive. Lotuses made of jewels appear on Vulture Peak, near where the Buddha is teaching, and the bodhisattva Manjushri asks what they mean. Someone is coming, the Buddha says, from a far-off world: a bodhisattva named Gadgadasvara. And before he sets out, his own Buddha gives him a piece of travel advice that would do anyone good, on any trip, to any place that looks rougher than home.
screen: `JEWELED LOTUSES ON THE PEAK.` → `A VISITOR FROM FAR OFF.` → `ADVICE FOR THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the visitor. Gadgadasvara lives in a radiant world far away, and he himself is vast and shining. He wants to come and see Shakyamuni and the bodhisattvas around him, and hear this teaching. Second, the advice. His own Buddha tells him, in effect: when you go there, don't look down on that world. It is uneven, with hills and rough ground, and the beings there, even its Buddha and bodhisattvas, are small next to you. Don't think less of them for it. The sutra imagines our world from the outside, finds it bumpy and modest, and makes respect the visitor's first instruction. Third, the forms. When he arrives, a bodhisattva in the assembly asks what this visitor has done to be so radiant. The Buddha answers, then adds something more: this bodhisattva has taught the sutra in many forms. As Brahma and as Indra. As a king, a merchant, a householder. As a monk or a nun, a layman or a laywoman, a boy or a girl. Even among beings in the hardest realms. Whatever form would let someone hear, that is the form he takes. Fourth, the thread back. This is the skillful means from the start of the sutra, now walking around in a body. The teaching doesn't wait for people to come to its shape; it takes theirs. And in Kumarajiva's Chinese, the visitor's name is Wonderful Sound.

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who might need some help this week, and ask gently: what form would help actually take for them? Maybe a listener, maybe someone who fixes the leaky thing, maybe someone who leaves them in peace for an afternoon. Let the answer come, even if it isn't the role you like playing best.

Your line: many forms. Help takes the shape of the one being helped. See you tomorrow.

1180.title: The universal gate (Kern ch. 24)
1180.hook: Avalokiteshvara hears every cry and comes in whatever form is needed
1180.howItsDone: Avalokiteshvara is honored across Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism; people call on the bodhisattva's name in danger and distress, and this chapter of the Lotus Sutra is recited as a teaching on compassion that hears.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gadgadasvara, the visitor who teaches in many forms and was told not to look down on our rough world. Your line: many forms.

A cry for help doesn't have to be loud. A text at two in the morning that only says: you up? A long pause on a phone call. A friend who says I'm fine a little too quickly. Chapter twenty-four, in Kern's numbering, is about a bodhisattva whose whole work is hearing cries like that. You met him in year one, in the Heart Sutra. Here the bodhisattva Akshayamati rises, bares one shoulder in respect, and asks the Buddha: why is this one called Avalokiteshvara?
screen: `A CRY CAN BE QUIET.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT A NAME.` → `THE UNIVERSAL GATE.`

segments.voice: First, the answer. If beings in any kind of suffering hear this bodhisattva's name and call on it, the Buddha says, Avalokiteshvara hears them, and they are freed. Second, the dangers, one by one, like a list of nights nobody wants to have. Someone thrown into a great fire, and the fire does not burn. Someone swept along by a river, who finds shallow ground. Sailors blown toward an island of fierce spirits. A prisoner under the executioner's sword, and the sword breaks. Chains that loosen. A caravan on a road full of bandits, where the leader tells everyone to call the name together. The chapter turns inward too: those burning with desire, anger or confusion are freed by keeping this bodhisattva in mind. Third, the forms. Like yesterday's visitor, Avalokiteshvara comes in whatever shape a person can be helped by: as a Buddha, as Brahma, as a merchant, a monk, a child. Kern's English calls the chapter the all-sided one. The Chinese title, rendered in English as the universal gate, pictures it another way: a gate open on every side. Fourth, the necklace. Akshayamati takes off a necklace of pearls worth a great deal and offers it. Avalokiteshvara won't take it, until the Buddha asks him to accept, out of kindness to the giver. Then he divides it in two, and gives one half to Shakyamuni and the other to the stupa of the ancient Buddha Prabhutaratna. The one who hears keeps nothing for himself.

segments.voice: Let a recent hard moment surface, a small one is enough, and let it be there without fixing it. If you're a Buddhist who calls on Avalokiteshvara, say the name softly now; if not, simply breathe as if someone were listening fully to that moment, with no hurry and no judgment. Stay with it, breath by breath, and let the listening be wide.

1181.title: Guanyin's chapter chanted (Kern ch. 24)
1181.hook: this chapter is chanted alone across East Asia
1181.tomorrow: The king and his sons (Kern ch. 25)
1181.howItsDone: In Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese Buddhism, the universal gate chapter is recited on its own as a short scripture, and people call on Guanyin with the chant Namo Guanshiyin Pusa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the universal gate: Avalokiteshvara, who hears every cry and comes in the form that's needed. Your line: the one who hears.

On a temple bench, or at a small shrine on top of a kitchen cabinet, a few people sit with a thin booklet open and chant together. The booklet isn't the whole Lotus Sutra. It's one chapter, yesterday's, traveling on its own. In Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese Buddhism, the universal gate is recited as a short scripture of its own. You met Guanyin last year; this time, stay with yesterday's chapter, and listen to how it is used.
screen: `A THIN BOOKLET ON A BENCH.` → `ONE CHAPTER, TRAVELING ALONE.` → `HOW IT IS USED.`

segments.voice: First, a chapter that became a book. Printed and chanted on its own, it is often called the Guanyin Sutra in Chinese, and in Japanese the Kannon-gyo. People recite it at home and in temples, in times of illness and fear, and on ordinary mornings. Second, the names. Guanyin is the Chinese name for Avalokiteshvara. The fuller form, Guanshiyin, is the name in Kumarajiva's Chinese Lotus, and it is usually rendered: the one who perceives the sounds of the world. In Japan the name is Kannon, in Korea Gwaneum, in Vietnam Quan Am. And here yesterday's many forms come back. In Indian art the bodhisattva appears as a princely male figure; in Chinese art Guanyin is often shown as a woman in white robes. Some Buddhists in these traditions say the same compassion takes whatever form people can receive. Third, the verses. The chapter closes with verses that retell its promises in rhythm, easy to carry in the mouth. Someone pushed into a pit of fire calls the name, and the fire becomes a pool. Someone pushed off a mountain stays in the air, like the sun. The verses are full of falling and being held. Fourth, chanting as listening. The chapter is about a bodhisattva who hears. The people who chant it are calling out, and they are also practicing hearing: the sound in the room, the voices beside them, their own breath between lines. Some who chant it describe this as being heard and learning to hear, in the same breath.

segments.voice: If you chant, say Guanyin's name the way it is said in Chinese temples, Namo Guanshiyin Pusa, slowly, once on each out-breath; if you'd rather not chant a name, hum one long, low note instead. The sound is half the practice. The other half is listening as it fades, all the way to silence, before the next breath.

1182.title: The king and his sons (Kern ch. 25)
1182.hook: two princes lead their father to the teaching
1182.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, this chapter is taught as a story about the good friend, the person who leads another toward the teaching, and it ties back to the Medicine King chapter, since the two princes are revealed to be the Medicine King and his brother.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chapter of the Lotus that people chant on its own: Guanyin, who hears the world's cries. Your line: chanted everywhere.

Two young princes want to hear a Buddha teach. Their father, the king, follows a different teaching and isn't interested. So the boys go to their mother first, and her advice is unexpected. Don't sneak off, she says, and don't argue with him. Go to your father and show him something. Let him see, so his mind turns clear. That's chapter twenty-five of the Lotus Sutra, in Kern's numbering: a family story from a past age that runs backward from the way families usually work.
screen: `TWO PRINCES WANT TO GO.` → `THEIR FATHER ISN'T INTERESTED.` → `THEIR MOTHER SAYS: SHOW HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's what the sons do, as the chapter tells it. They rise into the air in front of their father and walk there, sit there, lie down there, as if the sky were a floor. Water and fire stream from their bodies. They grow vast, then small again. The king is astonished, and glad. Who is your teacher, he asks. A Buddha, they answer, teaching the Lotus not far from here. Then I want to see him too, says the king. Notice the direction. Teaching usually flows downhill, from parent to child. Here it runs uphill. The sons don't lecture their father; they show him, and let him ask. They also ask their parents' leave to become monks, and the chapter gives a picture for how rare it is to meet a Buddha: like a turtle adrift on the ocean, surfacing right into the hole of a floating log. Then the whole family goes. The king hears the teaching, and in time he leaves his throne to practice. Here's the chapter's heart. The king tells the Buddha that his two sons have been his good friends; they turned him around. The Buddha agrees: a good friend is a great cause, the one who leads another to see a Buddha and set out on the path. And the ending reveals who these people became. The two sons are the Medicine King, whose story came a few days ago, and his brother. A good friend, in this sutra, can be your own child.

1183.title: Samantabhadra's promise (Kern ch. 26)
1183.hook: the bodhisattva of practice promises to protect those who keep the sutra
1183.howItsDone: In East Asian Mahayana traditions Samantabhadra is honored as the bodhisattva of practice and vows, and temple images show him seated on a white elephant; communities that keep the Lotus Sutra read this chapter as his pledge to protect them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two princes walked on the air until their father asked who had taught them. Your line: the sons led the king.

The Lotus Sutra is nearly over when, in chapter twenty-six, a late guest arrives from a world far to the east, with a great company behind him. His name is Samantabhadra. He bows and asks the Buddha a practical question, the kind someone asks near the end of a long meeting. After you are gone, how will people get hold of this teaching? What does it take?
screen: `A LATE GUEST FROM THE EAST.` → `HIS NAME IS SAMANTABHADRA.` → `HOW WILL PEOPLE KEEP THIS?`

segments.voice: The Buddha answers with a short list. Roughly: be held in the care of the Buddhas, plant roots of goodness, join the company of those set on the path, and turn the mind toward freeing all beings. Then Samantabhadra makes his promise, and it's surprisingly concrete. Whoever keeps this sutra, he says, I will guard. When they walk and turn the teaching over in their mind, I'll come riding a white elephant with six tusks and stand before them. When they sit and reflect on it, I'll come again. And if they forget a line, even one word, I'll be there to give it back. He adds protective spells, so nothing harmful can find an opening, and the Buddha praises him. Look at what the promise is attached to. Not to being clever, not to being finished. To keeping: reading, remembering, turning the words over while walking. The protection follows the practice, step for step. In the traditions that honor him, Samantabhadra is the bodhisattva of practice, of vows actually carried out. It's the week's last day, so look back at the end of the Lotus. Spells to guard those who keep it. The Medicine King's offering. Gadgadasvara in many forms. Guanyin hearing every cry, in a chapter chanted on its own. Two sons leading a king. And now a bodhisattva on a white elephant. Week after week the Lotus has said: this is precious. This week it added: you won't be left alone with it.
